name: Nasreen
definition: Nasreen is a composite portrait of a Bidriware artisan and workshop assistant from Bidar city, Bidar district, in the Kalyana Karnataka region. She represents the lived experience of women in traditional craft families navigating workshop labour, household responsibilities, children's schooling aspirations and the economic pressures facing Bidar's centuries-old silver-inlay metalwork trade.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Nasreen works in her family's small Bidriware workshop in one of the old neighbourhoods near Bidar Fort, where the craft has been practised for generations. She assists with the black-oxidation finishing and polishing stages after the men complete the inlay work, earning around four to five thousand rupees a month when orders are steady. The workshop depends on government emporium orders, tourist purchases and occasional export consignments arranged through craft cooperatives, but demand has become unpredictable. Her husband, also a Bidriware craftsman, works on the silver-wire inlay, and together they manage household expenses that include rent, food, children's school fees and healthcare. Mornings begin early with cooking and sending the children to school, then she reaches the workshop by nine. Work continues until late afternoon, interrupted by breaks for namaz at home. She buys vegetables and provisions from the weekly market near the Dargah-e-Shareef, where Dakhni Urdu is the common language of bargaining. Income fluctuates with tourist seasons and craft-fair bookings, and the family has taken small loans from relatives during lean months when orders dry up.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Nasreen lives with her husband, two daughters aged twelve and nine, and a seven-year-old son in a rented two-room house in Bidar city's old quarter. Her husband's elderly mother lives with them and helps with cooking and minding the younger child when Nasreen is at the workshop. Marriage was arranged when Nasreen was nineteen, and she moved from her parents' home in a nearby lane to her husband's household. Her own schooling stopped after Class 7 when her parents needed her to help at home and saw no path forward for girls in their community beyond marriage. She is determined that her daughters finish at least their SSLC and perhaps continue to PUC, though the costs worry her. Her older daughter attends the government Urdu-medium high school nearby, and Nasreen walks her there each morning before heading to work. Her son studies at a Kannada-medium school that charges a small fee, chosen because the family hopes he might find government work someday. Household chores—cooking, washing, fetching water when the tap runs dry—fall mostly to Nasreen and her mother-in-law. Her husband's income is pooled with hers, but decisions about spending rest largely with him and his mother.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Nasreen's own schooling ended at Class 7 in an Urdu-medium government school, a common path for girls in her neighbourhood at the time. She can read Urdu fluently and some Kannada, and she regrets not continuing to high school, feeling it limits her ability to help her children with homework or navigate official forms. Her older daughter, in Class 7 now, attends the same government Urdu-medium girls' high school Nasreen once did, and the girl is a good student, regularly bringing home marks above seventy percent. The school charges no tuition, but Nasreen pays for textbooks, uniform cloth and the annual exam fee, amounting to around two thousand rupees a year. She dreams her daughter might study further, perhaps become a teacher, though the cost of PUC college and the question of whether the family can spare her labour at home loom large. Her younger daughter, in Class 4, studies at the same school. Her son, in Class 2, attends a nearby Kannada-medium school that charges a nominal fee; Nasreen and her husband chose Kannada for him hoping it opens government-job pathways under the Article 371(J) local-recruitment quota.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Nasreen delivered all three children at the government district hospital in Bidar city, and she takes them there for vaccinations and when they fall ill, though she sometimes consults a local Unani practitioner for minor ailments. The hospital is within walking distance, but waiting times are long and medicines often need to be purchased from outside pharmacies. Her mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure, managed with tablets from the government hospital's outpatient clinic, though the family sometimes struggles to afford the prescribed diet. Nasreen herself has experienced recurrent back pain from long hours bending over workshop tasks, but she rarely takes time off to see a doctor unless the pain becomes unbearable. The family is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat, and the card came in useful when her husband needed minor surgery two years ago, covering much of the hospital bill. Drinking water comes from a municipal tap in the lane, and Nasreen boils it during summer when stomach infections spread. She worries about her daughters' health as they grow older, particularly menstrual hygiene, which is rarely discussed openly at home. The workshop's dust and chemical fumes bother her lungs sometimes, but she has no protective equipment and considers it part of the craft's unavoidable conditions.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Nasreen's family belongs to Bidar's Muslim community, which has lived in the city for generations, tracing roots back to the Bahmani Sultanate period and the city's centuries as a Deccani cultural centre. The neighbourhood around the Bidar Fort and the old bazaar lanes is predominantly Muslim, with Urdu and Dakhni spoken at home and in the market. Her family visits the Dargah-e-Shareef of Khwaja Bande Nawaz in Kalaburagi once a year during the urs, a journey by KKRTC bus that the whole household looks forward to. Daily prayers structure the rhythm of life: her mother-in-law prays five times a day at home, and Nasreen joins for Fajr and Maghrib when workshop hours allow. Her husband sometimes attends Friday prayers at the neighbourhood mosque. Community ties are dense—relatives live within walking distance, and the lane's families have known each other for decades. Weddings, Eid celebrations and condolence gatherings bring everyone together. Nasreen's circle includes other Bidriware artisan families, and women gather in the afternoons to chat, share news and help with each other's children. She is acutely aware of the stereotypes that outsiders sometimes hold about the region being "not really Kannada" because of its multilingual character, and she feels both pride in Bidar's Deccani heritage and frustration that this history is sometimes read as foreignness rather than as rooted Karnataka identity.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Nasreen has a ration card and an Aadhaar card, and the family collects subsidised rice and kerosene each month from the ration shop near the market. She enrolled for the Gruha Lakshmi scheme when it was announced, and the monthly two thousand rupees deposited directly into her bank account has become an important cushion for household expenses, though she wishes it were indexed to inflation. The family's Ayushman Bharat card came through the local Asha worker's help, and Nasreen keeps it carefully for hospital visits. She has heard of Article 371(J) and the special status meant for Kalyana Karnataka, and she hopes her son might one day benefit from the local-recruitment quota in government jobs, though she does not fully understand the domicile-certificate process. Her husband applied for a loan under a craft-cooperative scheme, but the paperwork took months and the amount granted was less than hoped. Nasreen has never voted separately from her family's collective decision, usually guided by her husband and his brothers, though she is registered as a voter. She is aware of the annual September 17th event marked by some as Liberation Day and by others in her community as Integration Day, and the contested framings of Hyderabad State's end make her wary of political rhetoric that pits one memory against another. She has little direct interaction with the taluk office or the municipal corporation, except when renewing ration-card details or getting a birth certificate for her youngest child.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Nasreen worries most about money—whether the workshop will get enough orders, whether the children's school fees can be paid on time, whether a medical emergency will force the family into debt. She is proud of her craft and the centuries of skill it represents, but frustrated that Bidriware's reputation does not translate into steady income for artisans like her family. She wants her daughters to have choices she did not, and she is determined they finish schooling even if it means tight budgets and borrowing from relatives. She blames the government for not doing enough to support traditional crafts beyond token awards and exhibitions, and for letting tourist interest wane without serious marketing. She resents the way Bidar and the larger Kalyana Karnataka region are labelled "most backward" in reports, a phrase that feels like an insult rather than a diagnosis calling for remedy. She sees the multilingual, multi-faith character of her neighbourhood as a strength, not a deficit, and she bristles when outsiders imply the region is less authentically Kannadiga because Urdu and Dakhni are spoken here. She takes pride in Bidar Fort, the city's heritage and the memory of the Bahmani court, and she wishes her children knew more of this history in their textbooks. She hopes Article 371(J) will eventually deliver real opportunities for local youth, but she has seen enough schemes come and go to remain cautious. Above all, she wants her children to have a stable future, whether through education, craft or government work, and she is prepared to work as hard as necessary to give them that chance.
